name: Gracile and cuneate nuclei
summary: The gracile and cuneate nuclei sit in the dorsal lower medulla beneath the gracile and cuneate tubercles and receive the ascending fibers of the posterior columns: the gracile nucleus from the leg and lower trunk (fasciculus gracilis), the cuneate nucleus from the arm and upper trunk (fasciculus cuneatus). Their axons cross as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. The accessory cuneate nucleus, just lateral, sends unconscious proprioception from the arm to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

anatomy.location: Dorsal closed medulla just above the pyramidal decussation, medial (gracile) and lateral (cuneate) to each other under the tubercles that bulge into the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle region; the accessory cuneate nucleus lies lateral to the cuneate nucleus.

function: Second-order relay of discriminative touch, vibration and conscious proprioception; the site of the somatotopic hand-over from ipsilateral to contralateral representation.

bestView.label: dorsal closed medulla beneath the gracile and cuneate tubercles
dorsal surface of the lower medulla

imaging.normalAppearance: The tubercles form the posterior surface of the lower medulla on axial T2 and sagittal images; the nuclei themselves are not resolved. Subacute combined degeneration shows T2 hyperintensity of the posterior columns continuing up to this level.

pathology.finding: Small dorsal paramedian lesion at the cervicomedullary junction with ipsilateral loss of vibration and position sense.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 of the cervicomedullary junction

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception below the level
lesionEffects.mechanism: Fibers and nuclei are still uncrossed

lesionEffects.deficit: Sensory ataxia and pseudoathetosis of the hand

examination: Vibration and joint position sense compared side to side
Romberg and pseudoathetosis with eyes closed
Look for a sensory level for these modalities
pearls: A dorsal lesion at or below these nuclei gives ipsilateral proprioceptive loss; above them the loss is contralateral
Isolated numb clumsy hand can come from the cuneate fasciculus or nucleus (cervicomedullary demyelination)
